name: Serpentine Arête
approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FR 7601), hike the Colchuck Lake Trail ~4 mi / 2,280 ft gain to Colchuck Lake (5,574 ft). Round the lake's east/south shore, boulder-hop onto the Colchuck Glacier's lateral moraine, and traverse it toward the orange-colored rock marking the route start; 4th-class ledges lead up to a snow finger and the base of the technical climbing. Roughly 3 hours car-to-base at a brisk pace.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and the Colchuck Glacier moraine
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead (FR 7601) to Colchuck Lake: about four miles and 2,280 ft, taking a fit party with a rack roughly three hours, four if loaded. Stay left at the signed junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail and grind the rocky switchbacks to the lake at 5,574 ft. There is a pit toilet near the south end of the lake and this is the last easy water.

Work around the east and south shore, then boulder-hop up onto the crest of the Colchuck Glacier's lateral moraine as early as you reasonably can — staying low costs you time in loose scree. Once on the moraine, turn slightly left and follow it south/southeast toward the northwest face of Dragontail, roughly in the direction of the Colchuck-Dragontail col, gaining about another 1,000 ft above the lake.

Allow roughly an hour from the lake to the moraine crest and another stretch of boulder-hopping beyond that. Parties report about four hours car-to-base moving well.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep once the moat at the base has opened enough to step across; a snow patch can linger into early July
hazards: Moat between snow and rock at the base; axe and often crampons needed into early July
Loose scree and talus below the moraine crest
Rockfall on the lower route — a fatal-injury rockfall accident has occurred on the neighbouring Backbone Ridge, and parties above you are the main hazard
Afternoon thunderstorms are routine in summer on this face
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The whole face is one grey wall except for one thing, and that one thing is the start: a band of orange rock low on the northwest face. Trip reports call it the orange wall, the orange rock band, or the coloured pile of rocks — it is visible from the moraine well before you get there and it is the only strongly coloured rock at the base. Walk the moraine until you are directly under it.

Second confirmation, for when the base is in cloud and you cannot see colour: a distinct black tower stands roughly 500 ft up the wall above the start. If you can see a black tower above you, the ground beneath it is the right ground.

At the base you will normally have to deal with a moat between the snow and the rock — the transition off the snow finger onto granite is where an axe earns its keep, and parties who left crampons behind have regretted it into July. Above the moat, 4th-class ledges lead up through the orange band; the climbing turns 5th class almost immediately off the deck, so if you are still walking after several hundred feet you have started somewhere else.

Do not confuse this with Backbone Ridge, which starts about 200 ft away and roughly 200 ft lower on the same face, on low-angle bushy ramps. If the ground in front of you is vegetated ramp systems trending left, that is Backbone. Serpentine's start is bare orange rock that goes up.
